stimuli.text: A block of mass 5 kg on a 37° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 5 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.1. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.6 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.09\cos(6t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) and a hoop (I = MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.4 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 90 N/m and 60 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 1.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.
Both springs share the load.
The force is the weight, mg.

questions.stem: A 4 kg cart moving at 6 m/s collides with and sticks to a 7 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: The carts share the momentum.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

questions.explanation: v_f = 4·6/11 = 2.18 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 45.8 J.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 90 m wide, moving at 3 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 1 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 130 kg load 26 m at constant speed in 8 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
P = W/t.
Correct. P = mgh/t.

questions.stem: Masses of 10 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Use T = m₂(g + a).
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.

questions.stem: A planet has 10 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
The ratio is inverted.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².
g decreases with radius.

questions.stem: A 5 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 5 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Friction opposes the motion.
Include friction on the table block.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 30° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
Friction acts up the slope.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall at 13 m/s and rebounds at 4 m/s. The contact lasts 0.04 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Divide by time.
Include the rebound.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 380$$ N/m is compressed 0.19 m and launches a 0.1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
The ½ appears on both sides.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 47 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 15 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
Recheck the average.

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -100x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.
Correct. ω = √100 = 10 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.

questions.stem: A 54 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Check the direction of the acceleration.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
Include gravity.
The acceleration changes the normal force.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 5x^3$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 3$$ m?

options.why: Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
The force is not constant.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 110 m is banked so that a car at 23 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Square the speed.
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).
Measure the angle from the horizontal.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 11 m high at 14 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Take the square root for the time.
Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.03\cos(6t)$$ m. What is its maximum acceleration?

options.why: Multiply by the amplitude.
Correct. a_max = Aω².
That is v_max.
Differentiate twice: Aω².

questions.stem: A 1000 kg car heading east at 19 m/s collides with a 2000 kg car heading north at 10 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 4t^3 + 3t^2 - 2t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 2$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 24t + 6, so at t = 2 the value is 54.

questions.stem: A 0.8 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 195$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
The ratio is m/k.
That is the frequency.
Include the 2π.

questions.stem: Point masses of 2 kg and 3 kg are at the ends of a massless rod 3 m long. What is the rotational inertia about the rod's center?

options.why: Each mass is L/2 from the center.
Square the distance.
Measure from the center, not an end.
Correct. Sum of mr² with r = L/2.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 5$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: The rod is not uniform.
Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.

questions.stem: A uniform 3 m beam weighing 500 N rests on supports at both ends. A 700 N load sits 2 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
The load is not at the center.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.2 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.
The weight acts at L/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 1x^3 - 12x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Take the square root.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 2 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$2 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$5 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: A solid sphere rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 3.9 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅖MR².
That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 4 rad/s and amplitude 0.05 m. What is its speed when it is 0.03 m from equilibrium?

options.why: That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Use A² − x² under a square root.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 4 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital speed to A's?

options.why: Correct. v = √(GM/r), so v ∝ r^(−1/2).
Farther satellites move more slowly.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 7 m down a 20° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Friction removes energy.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.

questions.stem: A 6 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 6t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 2$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Divide by the mass to get speed.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 16 N·s; v = J/m = 2.67 m/s.

questions.stem: A car moving at 17 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 8 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Δx = v₀²/(2a).
Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.
Divide by 2a, not a.
That is the stopping time in seconds.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 15 m/s at 60° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight?

options.why: Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
Use v₀ sin θ.
That is the time to the top; the flight is twice as long.
Use the vertical component.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 7.5 m/s, v₀y = 13 m/s. T = 2v₀y/g = 2.65 s.

questions.stem: A 1 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 6 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 2.45 m/s².

questions.stem: A 3 kg ball moving at +8 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 5 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 5 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: That would be a sticking collision.
Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
Kinetic energy is conserved too.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -2 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 6 m/s.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$6 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$3 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Take the square root.
Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 16 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
The exponent is 3/2.
T² ∝ r³.
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).

questions.stem: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1.4 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle its speed is 4 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Correct. At the top, T + mg = mv²/r.
Centripetal force uses v².
Include gravity.
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m spins at 20 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.75 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: The clay's inertia is mR².
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
Use rotational inertias, not masses.

questions.stem: A 5 g bullet moving at 460 m/s embeds in a 3.2 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
Find the block's speed after the collision first.
h = V²/(2g).

questions.explanation: V = 0.718 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.0263 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 5 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.09 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
